narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A Cameroonian music historian or dance practitioner with expertise in Sawa culture.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Beat That Conquered the World: The Story of Makossa
This is makossa. 20th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (-NyJDecUdSE)
Title card: makossa · Cameroon · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Makossa originated in the 1950s in Douala, Cameroon, coined by Nelle Eyoum.
It developed from the confluence of traditional Sawa rhythms like assiko and ambasse bey with international influences including highlife, Congolese rumba, and funk.
on_screen: Map: Cameroon · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Makossa serves as a form of social expression and celebration.
The term 'kossa' functions as a stimulus to increase the fervency of the dance, reflecting a desire for cultural sovereignty and modern urban identity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:Female Makossa Dancer - Enugu State - Nigeria.webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Female_Makossa_Dancer_-_Enugu_State_-_Nigeria.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by energetic, suggestive hip movements and contortions.
It is performed to stimulate high energy on the dance floor, particularly during the frenzied 'secousse' parts of a song.
Watch for secousse.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (-NyJDecUdSE)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music features a strong electric bass rhythm, prominent brass sections, and syncopated guitar work.
Percussion often includes the bottle as an idiophone.
Listen for the electric bass, brass section, guitar, bottle (idiophone).
The pulse is 4/4 at about 150 beats a minute.
A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by syncopated guitar picking, prominent brass stabs, and a rhythmic, percussive use of the bottle.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Soul Makossa — Manu Dibango; Zamina mina (Zangalewa) — Golden Sounds; Soul Makossa — Manu Dibango (1993)
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: syncopated bass-driven groove

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically associated with urban 'palm wine bars' and popular balls known as 'bol' in Douala.
It evolved in settings where electricity and modern musical equipment became available to local musicians.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Nelle Eyoum, Manu Dibango, Eboa Lotin, François Missé Ngoh, Sam Fan Thomas, and Toto Guillaume.
Makassi is a lighter, more commercial variant of makossa popularized by Sam Fan Thomas in the 1980s.
Makossa is an evolutionary offshoot of traditional Sawa rhythms (assiko, ambasse bey, essewe) influenced by Congolese rumba, Ghanaian highlife, and American funk/disco.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: makossa is parent of assiko: Makossa is considered a slowed-down, modernized version of assiko.
makossa is parent of ambasse bey: A traditional Sawa rhythm that influenced the development of makossa.
makossa is sibling of soukous: Similar musical structure, though makossa is distinguished by its specific bass and brass focus.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.sound_description: A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by syncopated guitar picking, prominent brass stabs, and a rhythmic, percussive use of the bottle.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of makossa (Cameroon). Meter 4/4. Tempo about 150 bpm. Rhythm pattern: syncopated bass-driven groove. Instruments: electric bass, brass section, guitar, bottle (idiophone), drum set. Vocal style: lead vocalist with backup choir. Mood: energetic, frenzied, rhythmic. It should sound like this: A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by syncopated guitar picking, prominent brass stabs, and a rhythmic, percussive use of the bottle. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
